full_judgment:
This Appeal is at the instance of the defendants and arises out of a suit for establishment of title and recovery of khas possession of a certain piece of land.

2. The plaintiffs case is that the disputed land was originally held and possessed by one Zarif Khan in occupancy raiyati right on payment of half of the produce of the land as rent under the landlord Jogendra Kumar Chandra Zarip Khan died leaving two sons Rasha Khan and Akbar Khan as heirs, of whoa Akbar died leaving a daughter Shamsunnessa and brother Rashid as heirs. Rashid sold hit interest to the plaintiff by a registered Kabala dated 22-10-69. Subsequently Shamsunnessa also sold her interest in the land to the plain tiff by another Kabala dated 22-7-63. Whiff the plaintiff had been in possession, he has been dispossessed in it70 R. C by the defendants who have no right, title and interest it land in suit. The suit was contested by the defendants Nos. 1 and 4 by filing a statement in which it was, contended that Zarip Khan was a mere bargadar under Jogendra Kumar Chandra and his four brothers and the C. S record was wrongly prepared in the name of Zarip Khan as a raiyati. Zarip Khan while cultivating the land as a bargadar surrendered the same in favour of the Chandra brothers among whom there was an amicable partition whereby Bhupendra, Upeadra and Narendra got the disputed land in their Saham Subsequently Bhupendra and Nagendra sold their 2/3rds share in the same land to one Monoranjan Chakrabarty by a Kabala dated 11- 2-31. Monoranjan also took oral raiyati settlement of the remaining 1/3rd share from Upeandra Kumar. Monoranjin having been in possession of the chsputeo land since his purchase entrusted the management of the suit property to the defendant No 4 after partition of the country when he went to India and since then defendant No. 4 has been possessing the suit land. The plaintiff or his predecessors had no possession in the land has been further asserted in the written statement that Monoranjan contracted to sell the suit land to the defendants in Baisakh, 1370 B. S, and took earnest money from him.

3. On the basis of the aforesaid pleading certain issues were framed and both parties have adduced oral and documentary evidence in support of their respective cases.

4. One of the points urged in the Trial Court was with respect to the interest of the Chanda brothels. The plaintiff contended relying upon the C. S. Khatian No. 517 (Ext. 2(C) and Khatian No. 414 Ext. 2 (d) Jogendra Chanda alone was the owner of the land under whom Zarip Khan was an occupancy raiyati whereas the defense case was that the land belonged to Kashi Chanda, the father of Jogendra and therefore all the Chanda brothers who were the sons of Kashi had interest in the land. The Trial Court on a consideration of the evidence on record came to the finding that the suit had originally belonged to Jogendra father and as such after Kashi's death, all of his six sous got the land by right of inheritance The 'la 'al Court a took the view that no presumption could be attached to the entry of the C. S. Khatian Ext. 2(h) as into evidence has been adduced to show the has of the entry of the said Khatian. Thereafter on an analysis of the evidence of both parties and the documentary evidence adduced in this case the learned Munsif held that the plaintiff did not acquire any title to the suit of his alleged purchase and that his allegation as to possession was not true. He came to the conclusion that the plaintiff also failed to prove his allegation of dispossession in the middle of Poush, 1370 B.S and Monoranjan was the real owner of the land and as such the plaintiff having had no valid title to the suit land was not entitled to get khas possession of the suit land.

5. On an appeal being taken by the plaintiff, it was heard by the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge Dacca and the learned Subordinate judge held that the learned Munsiff was not justified in rejecting the C. S. Khatian as evidence of title and possession of Zarip Khan in respect of the disputed land. According to the learned Subordinate Judge the plaintiff and accreted good title by virtue of the registered executed by the successor in interest of Zarip Khan He dis-believed the defense case of Monoranjan the owner of the land on the ground that the Kabala Ext. D evidences sale of rent-receiving interest only and that no documentary  fahdeaceead been adduced to prove the alleged oral sentiment of the refraining share of the disputed land by Upendra Kumar in favour of Monoranjan He referred to the evidence given by the witnesses of both parties and on a consideration of the same accepted the plaintiff's ease and held that the plaintiff's case of title and possession and dispossession had been sufficiently proved and that the earned Munsif was not justified in dismissing the suit The appeal was allowed and the plaintiff's suit was decreed on the basis of the aforesaid findings.

6. The present appeal has been filed by the contesting defendant Nos. 1 and 4 and Mr. Pathan Shafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants submits that the court of appeal below erred in law in misconstruing the deed Ext D and in holding that only tent receiving-interest has been transferred by the said deed and the failure of the kerne Subordinate Judge to properly appreciate the nature of the document has vitiated the ultimate decision in the appeal The earner  Advocate further submits the learned Subordinate Judge having Nike to lake woke as certain documentary evident on record namely, Eels B. B (1) and Ext. C series the merits of the decision have been seriously affected. The next point urged by the learned Advocate for the appellants is than while assessing the oral evidence on record the court of appeal below has failed to notice the discrepant in the evidence of the plaintiff's witnesses as have been taken into consideration by the Trial Court, and therefore the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge is not a proper Judgment of reversal.

7. Mr. S M. Haque, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents at the very outset pointed out that the view which has been taken by the learned Munsiff on the question of presumptive value of the C. S. Khatian Ext 2(VI) is not correct and this submission of the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents appears to be justified. Any party who relies upon the entries of a Settlement Khatian is not under any obligation to adduce evidence to prove the basis of the said entry. Of course, if on a production of some evidence it can be shown that there was no basis for the entry in the C. S Khatian to say that the said entry is contrary to or not supported by the basic document which may have been referred to in the Khatian itself, in  case it can be rightly argued that the Khatian has no basis and therefore no presumptive value can be attached to the same but ordinarily the entries in the C. S. Khatian shall have statutory  presumption of correct news in respect the stale of tutus indicated by the said entries. irrespective of the fact whether the person relying upon the said entries adduce any evidence in support thereof or not la this case the entries in the said C. S. Khatian shall raise a presumption in favour of the occupancy tenancy right of Zarip Khan as shown in the said C S Khatian It is for other side who chooses to dispute the correctness of the said entries to adduced evidence to show the contrary. In that view of the matter the learned Munsif ought to have approached the consideration of the evidence on record from the standpoint It is however, found that there are materials on record which can be taken onto consideration for the purpose of examining the question whether the presumption raised by the entries in the Khatian have been sufficiently rebutted by the said materials or not and although the learned Munsif made an error in attaching the proper presumptive value to the entries in the C. S. Khatian he had applied his mind to the other evidence on record on the question of title and possession of the land.

<u>8. As regards the first point urged by the learned Advocate for the appellant that the learned Subordinate Judge has misconstrued the Kabala Ext. (1), I find that this contention has some justification. The learned Subordinate Judge is not correct in holding that the Kabala was merely a deed for the purpose of transfer of the rent-receiving-interest of the vendors. Rather, it appears from an examination of the contents of the document that was purported to have been demised by the said deed was the land itself, which was alleged to have been in actual possession of the vendors. As regards the second point also I find that the learned Subordinate Judge has not given any consideration to the documents Ext. Nos. 8, 13(1 ) and C series for the purpose of ascertaining the actual position with regard to possession of the &sported land. Ext. B is a copy of the Order sheet in a proceeding under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, Est. B 1) is a carotids copy of an order in a Criminal case brought by the plaintiff as against the defendant No 1 whereby the case under section 379 P.P.C. was dismissed and Ext. C series are the rent-receipts in respect of payment rent on behalf of Monoranjan in respect of Khatian No. 446/1 which included the disputed C.S. plot No 196 till the record was corrected by subsequent order of the Revenue authority. These rent-receipts also have some bearing upon the question of possession. With regard to the third point also find that the learned Advocate for the appellant is right in his contention that the discrepancies in the testimony of the plaintiff's witness as have been noticed by the learned Munsif and also certain admission made P W. 2 which weighed with the learned Munsif for his conclusion have not at all been taken notice of by the appellate Court. In my opinion, the failure of the learned Subordinate Judge to advert to the documents and also to the discrepancies and other points mentioned above have vitiated the judgment of the lower appellate Court and therefore the said Judgment is not sustainable in law One of the questions involved in this case pertains to a claim of a right of tenancy by a bargadar and the position of bargadar under the old system was anomalous. There was no bar against a bargadar having a right of tenancy under the Bengal Tenancy Act, and although in 1929 by an amendment of provision relating to the definition of a tenant, a legal presumption that a bargadar is not tenant was sought to he introduced, but by adding a proviso to the amending legislation it was made clear it could still he shown by producing evidence in a court that the bargadar had a right of tenancy and was not merely an agricultural labourer engaged for cultivation of land and growing crops thereon. The same definition has been adopted in the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The legal import of this definition was considered and explained in a Division Bench decision of the Dacca High Court in the case of Kumir Mandal and others Vs Pramatha Nath Chowdhury and others, reported in 14 DLR 830 and by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in an appeal from the said decision in the case of Pramatha Nath Chowdhury and others Vs Kumir Mandal and others, reported in 17 DLR (SC) 392 same case PLD 1965 (Supreme Court) 434. In a Division Bench decision of this court in the case of Sona Mia and others Vs. Momraj Bhuiyan and others, (Second Appeal No. 920 of 966 decided on 8 3.7 to which I was party it has been pointed out that it is ultimate a Civil Court which will have to decide the question as to a bargadar having a right of tenancy, if such a question is raised, on the basis of the materials on record after paying due regard to the presumption which mar be raised by some entries in a Settlement Khatian.</u>

The evidence on record requires fresh assessment from the correct standpoint and after giving due consideration to the materials on record.

I therefore, allow this appeal and set aside the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court and remand the same to the sail court for rehearing of the appeal according to law and in the light of the observations made above. The cost of this appeal will abide the result. Let the records be sent down expeditiously.

End.
